transport: VE.Bus (RS-485 daisy chain, proprietary framing) over RJ45 to a MultiPlus/Quattro. Not addressable by third parties.
refutedOnReview: REFUTED — not because the two units differ, but because the entry asserts a shared *register map* at `vendor-doc` confidence when no cited source states a register map for either model, and its own evidence text concedes "there is no map to share."  **What checks out** - Both part numbers are real Victron order codes. `REC020005010` = Digital Multi Control 200/200A; `DMC000200010R` = Digital Multi Control 200/200A GX
gotchas: Victron's protocol overview table states plainly that VE.Bus third-party connections are 'No'. Their words: 'The synchronization feature is mission-critical. Direct third-party connections are not allowed.' This is not a licensing nicety — putting another talker on the bus breaks parallel and three-phase sync.

'Even at Victron we are not talking directly to VE.Bus' — the whitepaper notes that the Color Control GX and the VE.Bus-to-NMEA2000 interface both contain an MK2/MK3 IC. Any route to a MultiPlus goes through a GX, an MK3-USB, or a VE.Bus-to-CANbus interface.

The 'GX' in the DMC part number is a Victron model-naming suffix for the redesigned enclosure. It does NOT mean the panel is a GX device, does not mean it runs Venus OS, and does not mean it speaks anything a GX speaks. Filed here specifically so the name does not mislead a future reader.

The MK2/MK3 protocol IS publicly documented ('Interfacing with VE.Bus products – MK2 Protocol', rev 3.14) and does allow reading, on/off, current limits and configuration — but Victron warns 'implementing the MK2/MK3 protocol is a task which is not to be underestimated... unless there is a huge commercial interest, we
One MK2/MK3 or one VE.Bus-to-NMEA2000 interface serves an entire VE.Bus system, however many units are paralleled — not one per unit.
